note: Documents which groups have actually been harmed by educational algorithms, useful evidence for an education sector engagement.
title: Algorithmic Bias in Education
journal: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education

reading.body:
The best-documented harms from educational algorithms fall along race or ethnicity, gender, and nationality, while poorer students, students with disabilities, and military families are far less studied.

That gap is the finding. A review of this kind can only report what the literature has measured, and the literature has concentrated on a few categories of students. The groups with the least evidence are not necessarily the least harmed. They are the ones nobody has looked at closely enough to say.

Education is where algorithmic decisions attach to a person's record early and stay there. A placement, a score, or a flag follows a student through school. That makes undetected bias in these tools different from bias in a recommendation feed, and it is why the authors argue for moving from fairness in the abstract toward equity in outcomes.

The paper is a review, not a measurement. It does not establish how often any tool harmed any group, and it does not quantify the size of any effect. It also predates the current wave of generative systems in classrooms, so its evidence base covers the algorithms that came before them. What it offers is a map of where bias enters development and deployment, and a clear statement of which students the field has failed to study.

explain_beginner: This review looks at bias in computer systems used in education. It gathers existing evidence about which groups have actually been harmed. The most studied groups are race or ethnicity, gender, and nationality. There is less evidence about students from poorer backgrounds, students with disabilities, and students from military families. The paper also examines where bias can enter when educational algorithms are built and used. It matters because schools increasingly rely on AI and other educational technology. If these tools treat some students unfairly, they can affect opportunities and outcomes. The authors call for a shift from not knowing where bias exists to identifying it, and from fairness toward equity. They note obstacles and suggest ways to reduce harm.
explain_business: For executives, this paper signals that educational AI and related technology can carry bias that harms particular student groups. The authors reviewed existing evidence and found that race or ethnicity, gender, and nationality are the best documented areas, while students from poorer backgrounds, students with disabilities, and students from military families are less understood. They also point to where bias can arise during development and deployment. In practice, leaders should not assume a tool is fair just because it is widely used. The paper supports decisions to demand evidence of unequal impacts, assess bias with appropriate metrics, address understudied groups, and invest in mitigation and equity efforts.
explain_practitioner: The paper is a review. It examines causes of bias in education, connects theoretical and formal fairness ideas to the steps used to build machine learning systems, and surveys metrics for measuring bias. Race or ethnicity, gender, and nationality have the most evidence. Students from poorer backgrounds, students with disabilities, and students from military families have less. The review identifies which stages and people in development and deployment are involved. Its contribution is a framework for moving from not knowing where bias exists to identifying it, and from fairness toward equity. It notes barriers and proposes four areas of work to reduce bias in AI and learning technology.
